final_proof:
Let
\[
\delta_n(x)=\frac{n}{\pi}\frac{1}{1+n^2x^2},\qquad n\in\mathbb N_{>0}.
\]
We prove that \(\delta_n\) converges in the sense of distributions to the Dirac distribution at \(0\).

First, each \(\delta_n\) is nonnegative and integrable. With the substitution \(u=nx\),
\[
\int_{\mathbb R}\delta_n(x)\,dx
=\frac1\pi\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{du}{1+u^2}
=\frac1\pi[\arctan u]_{-\infty}^{\infty}=1.
\]
Moreover, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), the mass outside \((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\) tends to zero. Indeed,
\[
\int_{|x|\geq\varepsilon}\delta_n(x)\,dx
=\frac1\pi\int_{|u|\geq n\varepsilon}\frac{du}{1+u^2}
\leq \frac2\pi\int_{n\varepsilon}^{\infty}\frac{du}{u^2}
=\frac{2}{\pi n\varepsilon}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Thus the functions have the normalization and concentration properties of a delta sequence.

It remains to verify the asserted distributional limit. Let \(\phi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)\) be arbitrary. Again substituting \(u=nx\) gives
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\phi(x)\,dx
=\frac1\pi\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\phi(u/n)}{1+u^2}\,du.
\]
For every fixed \(u\in\mathbb R\), continuity of \(\phi\) at zero yields \(\phi(u/n)\to\phi(0)\). Since a test function is bounded,
\[
\left|\frac1\pi\frac{\phi(u/n)}{1+u^2}\right|
\leq \frac{\|\phi\|_\infty}{\pi(1+u^2)},
\]
and the function on the right is integrable over \(\mathbb R\). The dominated convergence theorem therefore implies
\[
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{\mathbb R}\delta_n(x)\phi(x)\,dx
&=\frac1\pi\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\phi(0)}{1+u^2}\,du\\
&=\phi(0).
\end{aligned}
\]
By definition, the Dirac delta distribution \(\delta\) acts on test functions by \(\langle\delta,\phi\rangle=\phi(0)\). Since \(\phi\) was arbitrary, it follows that
\[
\delta_n\longrightarrow\delta\quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb R),
\]
as claimed.
